prompt.context: The client owns and operates 25 retirement apartment complexes for the 55–75 year old demographic in the south-east and south-west states of FL, CA, NM, and AZ. By and large the apartment complexes have a similar design and amenities.
prompt.question: Should the client company's CEO consider expanding to other Northern cities, or continue to focus on the South?

clarifying_info.q: What are the client's specific financial goals?
clarifying_info.a: Maximize profitability through new apartment complexes and/or existing properties.

clarifying_info.q: What makes the client think there is demand in the North?
clarifying_info.a: A survey conducted 2–3 years ago in states such as NY, NJ, MA, and IL revealed that pre-retirees and retirees want similar facilities in those underserved markets (no competition exists) so they can stay closer to their families and friends.

clarifying_info.q: Has the client tested the North at all?
clarifying_info.a: Yes. A pilot apartment complex was erected in downtown Chicago 2 years ago with more amenities than its sister properties in the South.

exhibits.title: Cost Comparison Table – North vs. South
exhibits.shows: A table listing monthly cost line items (Maintenance, Amenities, Utilities, SG&A, Medical Facility, Total Cost) side by side for a North property and a South property, along with Total Revenue and Profit per building per month.
exhibits.data: North: Maintenance $80,000 | Amenities $54,000 | Utilities $45,000 | SG&A $60,000 | Medical Facility $60,000 | Total Cost $299,000 | Total Revenue $360,000 | Profit $61,000. South: Maintenance $100,000 | Amenities $48,000 | Utilities $38,000 | SG&A $80,000 | Medical Facility $0 | Total Cost $266,000 | Total Revenue $320,000 | Profit $54,000.

exhibits.title: Profitability Analysis Guidance
exhibits.shows: Narrative guidance on computing profit margin for each region and comparing them, plus next-step considerations around capital costs and NPV.
exhibits.data: Profit margin formula: Profit per mo per building ÷ Total Revenue per mo. Both North and South yield approximately 16.8% margin.

framework: Understand the market: current South footprint, competition, occupancy trends, and whether an unmet market exists in the North
Assess revenue drivers: number of units, occupancy rates, rent per unit, premium amenities revenue
Assess cost drivers: maintenance, amenities, utilities, SG&A, medical facility (North only) — distinguish fixed vs. variable
Calculate absolute profit per building per month for North vs. South
Calculate profit margin (profitability relative to revenue) for each region
Compare capital cost / NPV of opening in the North vs. renovating/enhancing South properties
Synthesize: since financial metrics are roughly equivalent, strategic factors (first-mover advantage, risk, execution) should drive the recommendation

questions.prompt: What is the monthly profit per building for a North property versus a South property?
questions.guidance: Candidate should compute revenue first (units × occupancy × rent), then subtract total costs line by line. Strong candidates distinguish fixed vs. variable costs and note the medical facility is North-only. They should not stop at absolute profit but proceed to margin.

math.setup: Revenue = units × occupancy rate × monthly rent. Costs are given per line item. Profit = Revenue − Total Costs.
steps: South Costs: Maintenance $100,000 + Amenities $48,000 + Utilities $38,000 + SG&A $80,000 + Medical $0 = $266,000
North Costs: Maintenance $80,000 + Amenities $54,000 + Utilities $45,000 + SG&A $60,000 + Medical $60,000 = $299,000
math.answer: North: $61,000/mo profit; South: $54,000/mo profit per building.

questions.prompt: Which region is more profitable relative to revenue generated?
questions.guidance: Candidate must compute profit margin (profit ÷ revenue) for each region, not just compare absolute profit. A strong candidate recognizes both are roughly equal and uses this to shift the discussion to strategic considerations and capital cost analysis.

math.setup: Profit Margin = Profit per mo per building ÷ Total Revenue per mo
math.answer: Both North and South yield approximately 16.8% profit margin — essentially equivalent.

questions.prompt: Given equivalent margins, what additional financial analysis should be done before recommending North vs. South?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify that capital cost / NPV comparison is the next logical step: cost to build new properties in the North, cost to renovate or add medical facilities to existing South properties, and which initiative yields higher NPV. The casebook notes we will not explore capital cost in this case but acknowledges return on cost analysis is a required next step.

brainstorming.prompt: To increase profitability in the South, what strategic initiatives could the client consider?

categories.name: Revenue enhancement
ideas: Add 24-hr on-site medical facilities to Southern properties and charge a premium in rent, mirroring the Chicago model
Introduce optional premium amenity packages to capture higher willingness-to-pay among residents
Add retail or ancillary revenue streams within the complexes (pharmacy, wellness services)

categories.name: Cost reduction
ideas: Apply best practices learned at the Chicago pilot (e.g., efficient medical facility management) back to Southern properties
Re-negotiate vendor and maintenance contracts using scale across 25 properties
Optimize SG&A through shared services or centralized leasing and marketing functions
Benchmark utilities costs and invest in energy-efficient upgrades

categories.name: Occupancy / market defense
ideas: Proactively invest in amenity upgrades before competitors enter to maintain 90%+ occupancy
Differentiate on community programming to reduce churn and keep occupancy from settling at 80%
Targeted marketing to the 55–75 cohort who may be migrating South, leveraging the 3–5% annual inflow

recommendation: Expand into the North to capture the first-mover advantage in underserved markets (no current competition, demonstrated demand via survey, pilot validated in Chicago)
Simultaneously enhance Southern properties — specifically by adding on-site medical facilities and raising rent — to close the absolute profit gap and defend market share as competition intensifies
risks: 90% occupancy in the North may not be sustainable long-term; the South pattern shows occupancy declining to ~80% as new entrants build, and the same dynamic could emerge once the North market attracts competition

Capital cost of Northern expansion (land, construction in dense urban markets) may be materially higher than Southern expansion, potentially lowering returns relative to cost even if margins are equivalent
Commercial real estate headwinds (relevant in 2009 context) could affect financing availability and construction timelines
Adding medical facilities to 25 Southern properties is capital-intensive and operational complexity increases significantly
next_steps: Evaluate capital cost to open new buildings in the North and cost to renovate or add medical centers in the South; compare NPVs to determine which investment delivers better return on capital
Size addressable demand in major Northern cities (NY, NJ, MA, IL) to estimate how many properties the market can support and at what pace
Identify and formalize best-practice transfer between North and South to realize operational efficiencies across the full portfolio
Develop a phased expansion plan for the North, starting with 2–3 cities, to test replicability of the Chicago pilot before committing to a large-scale rollout
